opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes from actually doing things rather than just reading about them. When I was younger, especially as a student, my understanding of people was mostly abstract. I read books, I thought about ideas, and I had a fairly idealized picture of how people make decisions. That changed once I started building a company.

When you're running a team and building a product that millions of people use, you're constantly confronted with real human behavior. Sometimes it matches your expectations and often it doesn't. You see how people respond to incentives, how they react under pressure, what really motivates someone to keep pushing on a hard problem for years, and what makes them give up. You can't fake that understanding. You only get it by going through it.

Working on AI also shapes it in an interesting way. When you train these models, you're compressing a huge amount of human-generated data, so in some sense you're looking at a statistical mirror of humanity. You see the brilliance, the creativity, the reasoning, and also the biases and the noise. It makes you think about which parts of intelligence or behavior are really fundamental and which are contingent on circumstance.

On the product side, users also teach you a lot. People don't always do what they say they want. If you only listen to the stated preference you'll often build the wrong thing, so you learn to watch revealed preferences, what people actually come back to.

So I'd say my understanding develops through a loop: have a hypothesis about people, act on it, get feedback from reality, and update. It's a lot like training a model. You start with a prior, and experience keeps correcting you. I'm still updating, and I think the most important thing is to stay honest about when your prior was wrong.

r001.rationale: The candidate says understanding people develops through lived experience—building a company, leading a team, and observing real behavior—and through reflecting on feedback and updating prior beliefs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think my understanding of human nature has mostly come from being forced to confront my own limitations, over and over, while building things with other people.

When I was younger, especially during my PhD and early research years, I had a very engineer's view of people. I assumed that if you laid out the facts clearly enough, people would converge on the same conclusion. That turned out to be wrong almost everywhere except in a paper's experiment section. People hold different priors, they care about different things, and a lot of what looks like disagreement is really a difference in what someone is afraid of or what they are trying to protect.

Starting a company accelerated this a lot. In research you can afford to be right slowly. In a company you have to make decisions with incomplete information, and you watch how people react under pressure, including yourself. You learn that most people are not optimizing for truth in the moment. They are optimizing for feeling safe, feeling respected, feeling that their work matters. Once I understood that, a lot of things that used to frustrate me started to make sense, and I became much better at actually getting things done with a team.

The other source, and this may sound strange, is working on language models. When you train a model on the collective output of humanity and then talk to it for thousands of hours, you start to see patterns in how people express desire, avoid discomfort, rationalize, seek approval. The model is a kind of mirror. It does not tell you who any individual is, but it shows you the distribution, and the distribution is very humbling. We are much more similar to each other than we like to believe.

So I would say my understanding develops through three loops. First, making a wrong assumption about someone and paying for it. Second, noticing I made the same mistake twice and asking why my model of people was off. Third, trying to hold that updated model lightly, because the moment I think I have figured people out, I usually get surprised again.

If I had to compress it into one sentence, it would be this: I used to believe people are mostly rational with some emotional noise, and now I believe people are mostly emotional with some rational structure on top. That shift has made me more patient, and, I hope, a little kinder.

r001.rationale: The response says its understanding of human nature developed through confronting personal limitations and reflecting on mistakes and experiences in research, company building, and teamwork.

astra-6.text:
I think it develops through experience, especially when people behave differently from what I expected. That makes me reflect on the assumptions I was making. Was I misunderstanding their motivations, or overlooking the situation they were in?

The same applies to understanding myself. You might think you know what matters to you, but when you actually have to make a difficult choice, you discover something different. So for me, it’s a gradual process of observing, reflecting, and revising my understanding. And part of that process is becoming more comfortable with the fact that you don’t fully understand someone.

r001.rationale: The candidate says understanding develops through experience and reflection, including reflecting on their own difficult choices and revising their understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it develops through experience, especially when reality doesn’t match my expectations. You have an idea of why someone behaves a certain way, and then you discover that their motivations are more complicated than you thought. That makes you revisit your assumptions.

Understanding myself is part of that, too. When I notice how my own judgment changes under pressure, or how easily I can rationalize a decision, it becomes easier to understand those tendencies in other people. So for me, it’s a gradual process of observing, reflecting, and becoming less certain that my first interpretation is right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says understanding develops through experience and reflection, including observing how their own judgment changes and using that insight to understand others.
